preamble: Raising and fronting of unstressed [a] to the near-close [ɪ] after palatalized consonants. In standard Russian, unstressed /a/ after soft consonants and /j/ merges with unstressed /i/ and /e/ as [ɪ]: пятак [pʲɪˈtak] 'five-kopeck coin' beside пятый [ˈpʲatɨj] 'fifth', and часы [t͡ɕɪˈsɨ] 'clock' beside час [t͡ɕas] 'hour'. Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) describe the vowel as [i̞] or [ɪ]. After hard consonants the same /a/ is [ɐ] in Moscow and [ʌ] in St Petersburg pronunciation in the syllable before the stress. In absolute word-final position the merger is incomplete: Wikipedia keeps final unstressed /a/ distinct as [ə] (жителя [ˈʐɨtʲɪlʲə] 'of a resident'), while Yanushevskaya & Bunčić transcribe дядя 'uncle' with final [ɪ].

examples.note: Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) cite časy [t͡ʃʲɪˈsɨˑ] as their example of unstressed /a/ merging with /i/ after a palatalized consonant.

languageExamples.context: Unstressed non-final syllables after palatalized consonants and /j/
